chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
title: Thanks to the Smithsonian; disco, rock and jazz's neglect
summary: Willard says little is written about her; Nellie expresses gratitude, then regrets disco and rock taking work from musicians while jazz goes unrecognized.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It's important, Nellie, because there's so little written down about you. You've done so much and you've been involved with so many marvelous people, you've contributed so much, and you can't find you in a book.
A couple of the encyclopedias give some brief information, but someone wants to find out about you they can't find it written down. Now we have some information.

Well, I'm very glad of that. I'm very grateful that they gave me the opportunity of doing this interview, and I hope that -- well, before I make it on home, as the old folks would say -- and I'm not homesick. As I say,

I want to make heaven my home, but I'm not homesick. I do plan to really get back into things, but I must say too that there have been changes that have come about, and where it does make one a little bit -- you get a little disgusted, a little bitter about certain things, because I feel that there is a place for every type of music, every type of music there is a place for it. And of course, as the time -- as we -- the time that we're into now, this period that we're into now, with the disco, well this to me is a great discredit to the average musician, because many musicians are not able to get a job because of the disco scene, you see.

Before disco, of course it was rock and roll. Well, I don't put the rock and roll scene down, you know. It's not my bag, it wasn't my bag. It was certainly very far from my type of thing or my scene, and the people who created it and the people who were fortunate enough to get into the act at that time, who were fortunate enough to get with the people who were promoters and people who promote this thing, and that's how rock and roll got to be so big, it really just boomeranged like nothing I've ever seen, you know. And jazz has never had this, unfortunately. It really has never had this type of thing. And the thing that hurts, the thing that bothers me, is that seemingly some people don't consider jazz that important, you see. They know what it is. They know it is definitely a creative thing. I think one of the most creative forms of
music ever. It's the thing that's created right here in our own country, and it's unfortunate that it's not recognized as widely and as much as it is in other countries.
